summaries.summary: Propaganda aims to influence mindsets for a specific agenda, and Internet-era social network sharing lets campaigns reach very large audiences.
Propagandist news articles use techniques such as whataboutism, red Herring, and name calling, and fine-grained language analysis can yield more reliable, explainable systems.
The authors organised the NLP4IF@EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019 shared task on a corpus of news articles annotated with 18 propagandist techniques at fragment level.
Prior propaganda work mostly used article-level labels obtained by distant supervision, which inevitably introduces noise.
Computational argumentation addresses propaganda-related fallacies, including Argotario, whose by-product corpus has $1.3k$ arguments annotated with five fallacies.
Unlike prior work, this corpus uses 18 techniques on the same news articles and annotates minimal fragments rather than entire arguments.
The most relevant related work is the authors' parallel EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019 paper describing a corpus that is a subset of this shared task corpus.
The shared task uses 18 psychological and rhetorical propaganda techniques in news articles that can be judged intrinsically without external resources.
Loaded language uses words or phrases with strong emotional implications, positive or negative, to influence an audience.
Name calling or labeling labels the propaganda object as something the target audience fears, hates, finds undesirable, loves, or praises.
Repetition repeats the same message over and over again so that the audience will eventually accept it.
Exaggeration or minimization represents something excessively or makes it seem less important or smaller, such as saying an insult was just a joke.
Doubt questions the credibility of someone or something.
Appeal to fear/prejudice builds support by instilling anxiety and/or panic toward an alternative, possibly based on preconceived judgments.
Flag-waving plays on strong national feeling or group feeling, such as race, gender, or political preference, to justify or promote an action or idea.
Causal oversimplification assumes one cause among multiple causes and includes scapegoating blame transferred to one person or group without investigating complexities.
Slogans are brief, striking phrases that may include labeling and stereotyping and tend to act as emotional appeals.
Appeal to authority states a claim is true because a valid authority/expert supports it without other evidence, including non-expert testimonial references.
Black-and-white fallacy, dictatorship presents two options as the only possibilities or tells the audience exactly what actions to take.
Thought-terminating cliché uses short, generic words or phrases that discourage critical thought and meaningful discussion about a topic.
Whataboutism discredits an opponent's position by charging hypocrisy without directly disproving their argument.
Reductio ad Hitlerum persuades audiences to disapprove an action or idea by associating it with groups hated in contempt by the target audience.
Red herring introduces irrelevant material to divert attention from the points made and lead discussion away from the issue in dispute.
Bandwagon attempts to persuade the target audience to join an action because “everyone else is taking the same action”.
Obfuscation, intentional vagueness, confusion uses deliberately unclear words so the audience can form its own interpretation.
Straw man substitutes an opponent's proposition with a similar one and then refutes that instead of the original.
The shared task features two subtasks.
Fragment-Level Classification task (FLC) detects all propagandist text spans in a news article and identifies the technique applied in each span.
Sentence-Level Classification task (SLC) predicts propaganda or non-propaganda for a sentence containing at least one propagandist fragment.
Both tasks use free-text news articles from 36 propagandist and 12 non-propagandist news outlets, with 450 earlier articles and 47 additional annotated articles.
Training, development, and test partitions contain 350, 61, and 86 articles and 16,965, 2,235, and 3,526 sentences, respectively.
Table TABREF23 reports total instances per technique and percentages of total annotations for the training and development sets.
The shared task had a development phase with labeled training and development datasets and a testing phase with testing input.
Participants tried to achieve the best performance on the development set while a live leaderboard tracked submissions.
The test set was released, and participants had few days to make final predictions.
In phase 2, no immediate feedback was provided, and the winner was determined by test set performance.
FLC combines propagandist fragment identification and 18-way technique classification, using modified F$_1$ for partial span matching and per-technique F$_1$.
SLC is a binary classification task with imbalanced data, with standard F$_1$ as the official measure plus Precision and Recall.
The SLC baseline is logistic regression with default parameters using sentence length as a single feature, shown in Tables TABREF33 and TABREF34.
The FLC baseline generates spans and randomly selects one of the 18 techniques, with its inefficacy shown in Tables TABREF36 and TABREF41.
A total of 90 teams registered, 39 submitted 3,065 submissions, with 21 teams making 527 FLC submissions and 35 teams making 2,538 SLC submissions.
The authors overview approaches from participants' papers, with high-level summaries in Tables TABREF28 and TABREF29.
Team newspeak achieved the best FLC test results using 20-way word-level BERT classification, the uncased base model with 12 Transformer layers and 110 million parameters.
Team Stalin used data augmentation and synthetic minority class over-sampling for ELMo, BERT, and Grover representations fed into an LSTM.
Team CAUnLP used two context-aware BERT representations, subsampling for class imbalance, and experiments with BERT$_{BASE}$ and BERT$_{LARGE}$.
Team LIACC used hand-crafted features and pre-trained ELMo embeddings, observing a performance boost when dropping some negative examples.
Team JUSTDeep combined GloVe word embeddings, affection vectors, lexical features, and an ensemble of bi-LSTM, XGBoost, and BERT variations.
Team YMJA used fine-tuned BERT and created an ensemble of models via cross-validation inspired by kaggle sentiment analysis competitions.
Team jinfen used logistic regression with TF.IDF, BERT vectors, vocabularies, and readability measures.
Team Tha3aroon implemented an ensemble of three classifiers: two based on BERT and one based on a universal sentence encoder.
Team NSIT explored transfer learning models including various versions of ELMo, BERT, and RoBERTa.
Team Mindcoders combined BERT, Bi-LSTM and Capsule networks into one deep neural network pre-trained on related-task corpora such as emotion classification.
Team ltuorp used an attention transformer using BERT trained on Wikipedia and BookCorpus.
Team MIC-CIS used a voting ensemble for SLC and an LSTM-CRF multi-task neural sequence tagger for FLC, applying sentence- and fragment-level models jointly.
Team CUNLP used fine-tuned BERT approaches for SLC and a Bi-LSTM-CRF architecture with character- and word-level embeddings for FLC.
Team ProperGander used BERT with oversampling and cost-sensitive classification for imbalance, and BERT with Continuous Random Field stacked on an LSTM for FLC.
SLC test results are in Table TABREF33 and development results in Table TABREF34, with decreased F$_1$ values suggesting possible development set overfitting.
FLC results in Tables TABREF36 and TABREF41 are more stable across test and development sets, with MIC-CIS reaching third place without a development run.
The NLP4IF@EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019 shared task received 25 SLC and 12 FLC test submissions; SLC was easier, while FLC was more challenging.
The authors plan to make the schema and dataset publicly available beyond NLP4IF and hope the corpus interests Argumentation and Sentiment Analysis researchers.
Task 11 at SemEval 2020 is a follow up of this shared task and features two complimentary tasks.
One SemEval 2020 task is to identify propagandist text spans in a free-text article.
The other SemEval 2020 task identifies the specific propaganda technique in a text span already flagged as propagandist and its context.
This setting lets participants focus on binary sequence labeling for Task 1 and multi-class classification for Task 2.

This research is part of the Propaganda Analysis Project within the Tanbih project, developed by Qatar Computing Research Institute (QCRI), HBKU, and MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL).
The corpus for the task was annotated by A Data Pro, a company that performs high-quality manual annotations.
